# The Case of the Missing Sock

At 7:12 on a wet Tuesday in November, I removed a blue sock from the dryer and discovered that its companion had not come home.

The survivor was navy blue, marked near the cuff by a single green stripe. Its heel was beginning to wear thin, but not badly enough to justify retirement. It was, in other words, a perfectly serviceable sock, and that made its partner’s absence more puzzling. Important things disappear in memorable ways. Important things arrive with explanations, an unlocked door, a final unanswered message. Socks have less dignity. They vanish into the machinery of ordinary life and rarely offer a reason.

This was not the sort of loss that organizes an entire day around itself. Nobody was waiting in a station somewhere with the missing sock folded inside a pocket. No television crew had been assigned to cover its disappearance. Still, I found myself standing beside the dryer, holding one sock in each hand, feeling that the laundry had presented me with a problem I ought to solve.

My partner, Nora, was eating toast at the table. She looked up and said, “Do you need to call the police?”

“Not unless they’ve taken statements.”

I spread the surviving sock on the table beside my coffee. Its absent companion had apparently left no forwarding address. Somewhere between the washing machine and the drawer, it had slipped out of the recognizable world and become merely a missing sock. I did not yet know whether I would find it, but I intended to conduct an investigation, because a clean little mystery seemed preferable to a morning spent answering emails.

## Evidence

Laundry is an excellent place for faith. We place our clothes inside a machine, provide a measured quantity of detergent, select a program, and trust that the process will return everything more or less appropriately accounted for. The machine may produce a shirt three sizes smaller or recolor a pair of trousers a shade of bruised violet, but we accept these transformations as reasonable. Only socks, apparently, have freedom of movement.

I began with an inventory. The blue sock lay on the table while I searched the clean laundry basket, the floor beside the washer, and the space behind the radiator. It could not have gone far. This was not one of those houses where an object disappears into a vast territory of skirting boards and forgotten cupboards. We owned furniture. The radiator had a towel over it, and the towels were accounted for.

I retraced the sock’s journey through what I hoped were its last hours. It had come out of the dryer with the other clothes. I had carried a wicker basket into the bedroom. I had probably emptied it beside the bed, although I could not testify to this with certainty. I had folded shirts, put away trousers, and performed the small administrative tasks by which clean clothing becomes an organized wardrobe.

This was where the case became frustrating. I was both the last person to see the missing sock and the only person capable of describing what had happened to it. My testimony was secondhand, my memory selective, and my standards of identification vague.

A second complication arose when I returned to the drawer. We own several blue socks. There are dark blue work socks, lighter blue exercise socks, and blue socks with stripes of various colors. The missing one had possessed a green stripe, but apparently the stripe was not sufficiently exclusive. I held up three candidates and discovered that I was now searching not for a specific sock but for a sock in the general neighborhood of a memory.

## The Bag

The search led me to the canvas bag on the highest shelf of the closet. It was the kind of bag intended for laundry but increasingly employed as a repository for things that had not yet been classified.

Its drawstring is missing. One end is tied in a knot while the other trails away into a pocket designed for, among other things, the missing drawstring. The bag contains a solitary metal button, two foreign coins, a key of uncertain purpose, a receipt so old that its prices no longer look like prices, and several items I would not immediately recognize if anyone asked me to explain them.

A laundry bag has a special relationship with time. The objects inside it are not necessarily valuable, but they have survived a series of decisions not to throw them away. Each one represents an earlier version of me who imagined a future in which the button, the key, or the peculiar piece of hardware would become necessary.

I call this the archaeology of the practical. A proper museum displays objects selected for their historical importance. The laundry bag displays objects selected for their historical proximity to me. A key is never just a key there. It is a key I once found in a coat, a key carried from one apartment to another, a key I kept because throwing it away felt like abandoning a question to which I had not yet learned the answer.

Sometimes the key is obvious in retrospect. It opened a toolbox in a former home. The coins can pay for a parking fee. The button belonged to a shirt that developed a tear during an otherwise successful week. But most of the bag’s contents resist explanation. They are less archive than warning, evidence that practical decisions made under imperfect conditions can produce mysteries for our descendants.

I searched beneath a folded scarf and found a small blue sock.

For a moment, I was triumphant. Then I turned it over and saw a yellow stripe.

I placed it back in the bag. The discovery had less evidentiary value than hoped, though it did establish that the universe was willing to give me a blue sock without giving me the one I wanted. This is common in lost-and-found situations. The relevant object often appears, but only to make the absence clearer.

## The Open Window

The bedroom window had been open a few centimeters overnight. I had opened it because the room smelled faintly of rain and because, during the day, the radiator made the space feel more like a small boiler room than a place for sleeping. At night the air was damp and alive, carrying the mineral smell of wet pavement.

The window was an obvious suspect. It had opportunity, access, and a draft sufficient to encourage ambitions. A sock, given favorable wind and an unusually careless sock, could conceivably leave through the gap, catch on the sill, and drop into the courtyard below.

It could not climb over the fence, however. I want to be clear about this. Even in the most expansive fiction, a sock has no arms. It can flutter, snag, and fall, but it is poorly equipped for an independent journey across a neighborhood.

I leaned out and looked along the outer ledge. I saw a leaf, a bottle cap, and a small plastic bag caught in a crack in the masonry. The plastic bag was blue. For several seconds, it seemed possible that I had misunderstood the entire case and that the missing sock had been transformed into litter by a dramatic encounter with the night air.

It was not a sock.

“The plastic bag is a decoy,” Nora called from the bedroom.

“I’m aware.”

“You’ve been gone a while.”

“The investigation is proceeding.”

I closed the window and considered the courtyard. Someone could have carried the sock into another apartment, but why? A person who finds a damp blue sock does not usually stop to identify the owner. It joins the miscellaneous contents of a coat pocket, a junk drawer, or a pile of items waiting to be donated. The sock has not been taken by a villain. It has simply entered a world in which nobody was thinking about it.

I did not find it on the windowsill. I did not find it beneath the radiator or behind the curtains. The window remained a plausible location but ceased to be a useful one. This is often how domestic mysteries proceed: the suspect has opportunity but no distinctive evidence.

## The Mathematics of Two

Socks have always seemed vulnerable to philosophical confusion because of their arrangement in pairs.

A pair suggests completion. One plus one makes two, two makes a pair, and the pair can then be placed in a drawer where it remains, presumably, at rest. A single sock looks like an error. It appears to be half an object, an item awaiting correction. But a sock is fully itself when worn. It knows how to cover a foot, keep warmth around an ankle, and meet the heel without becoming confused about its responsibilities. Its lack of a companion does not make it incomplete. It only makes it unmatched.

Commercial socks have left and right, but that distinction is largely a matter of retail display. Anatomically, our feet are not so different that a blue sock refuses to cooperate with a black one. The left side and right side belong to the habits of packaging, not the natural order of the foot. A red sock on the left and a blue sock on the right does not signify a political alliance. It signifies that we put our socks on in the morning.

I have come to respect unmatched socks more than I once did. A mismatched pair can be warmer, more comfortable, or simply more available. One may be thinner for summer. One may have been washed too often and become exceptionally soft. When I am dressed late and searching for something adequate, I choose whichever socks are nearest, often without noticing whether they correspond.

The drawer where we keep our socks contains a hierarchy more elaborate than necessity requires. Dark socks are grouped together. Exercise socks are kept separate, perhaps because they are thinner and because their elastic edges inspire suspicion. There is a section for good socks, a section for socks that will survive being worn to the grocery store, and a section for socks whose future depends on the mood of the day.

The missing sock had escaped this modest bureaucracy. It had been part of a neat pair, and now it was a member of a new category: socks that may be reunited but should not be expected to be.

The laundry machine had formed an alliance with one sock and abandoned the other. The drawer, for the first time in months, was mathematically wrong.

## What the Machine Knows

I returned to the washing machine and considered whether it had eaten the sock.

This was not an unreasonable suspicion. A washing machine contains a drum, water, a door, and a complicated arrangement of metal and plastic through which an object might theoretically disappear. It has no visible shelves, no personal locker, and no obvious reason to retain one blue sock while releasing its companion. Still, machines are often blamed for domestic losses because they are the last people or machines to have been near the missing item.

I inspected the rubber door seal, the inside of the drum, and the space behind the machine where dust, coins, and several mysterious washers had accumulated. I found no sock. I found a hair, a coin, and a small collection of lint that made me wonder how much of the previous wash had become permanently incorporated into the machine.

The more I examined the washing process, the more obvious it became that the machine was not an accomplice. It was doing what machines do. It agitated clothing in water, lifted things briefly, released them, and repeated the process until a person selected a button marked “Cotton” or “Synthetics” or some other optimistic description of the material involved.

A sock can disappear in perfectly ordinary ways. It can slide inside a duvet cover during the transfer from washer to basket. It can become caught in the folds of a sheet. It can travel into the pocket of a pair of trousers and remain there through an entire evening. It can emerge at the far end of a fitted sheet, looking confused but otherwise undamaged.

A washing machine has no theory of reunion. It does not know that the blue sock and the blue sock were important to one another. It sees cloth, water, weight, and time. If the socks were separated, it had no reason to restore their relationship.

I looked at the surviving sock in my hand and felt briefly sorry for it, though the feeling was impossible to maintain for long. The sock was a sock. It was not waiting anxiously for a lost relative. It was damp, slightly warm, and shaped by the dryer into a form that would disappear as soon as I put it on.

## A Drawer of Mismatches

The drawer beneath the bed has become a small museum of incomplete decisions.

There is a glove whose partner may have been lost in a train station, or in a coat, or in the particular dimensions of a future winter. There are socks with holes large enough to admit a toe, socks with holes not yet large enough to qualify as serious, and socks whose colors have faded into suggestions of their original selves. A wooden spoon has somehow entered the drawer, along with a charging cable for a device I no longer own. None of these objects is expensive. Together, they form a portrait of postponement.

The missing sock had briefly made this disorder feel like evidence. Now it had made it feel like a condition. The drawer contained several things that had survived not because they were indispensable but because no occasion had yet forced a final decision.

I considered the blue sock’s future. It could be worn with another blue sock, if one appeared. It could be worn with a different color. It could be washed, dried, and returned to the drawer, where it would resume its life as an ordinary object rather than a mystery. If the hole in its heel became impossible to ignore, I could mend it or retire it. The drawer, like all archives, was full of objects waiting for a story to become more convenient.

There was an old brown wool sock in the back of the drawer that I recognized from an earlier era of my life. It had belonged to my grandfather, and it had been darned at the heel with a thick zigzag. He had taught me, when I was young, that a useful garment should not be discarded merely because it had survived a long time. I had not fully accepted the philosophy, but I had learned to respect it.

The brown sock was not valuable in the ordinary sense. It was too short in the foot, too stretched in the cuff, and too committed to a previous decade. I kept it for years after my grandfather died, partly from affection and partly from the belief that useful things should be allowed to remain useful. Eventually the wool had become brittle. I threw it away, and what I missed was not the object but the idea of the person who had repaired it.

This is one difficulty with turning everyday belongings into emotional monuments. The objects eventually leave. The meanings they carry are more stubborn.

These objects are not all valuable. They are reminders that the past continues to deposit things in the present without asking whether we have room.

The laundry bag holds the same kind of unfinished business. A missing button may be found in a pocket. A receipt may become useful as evidence of a purchase nobody can remember. A key may fit a lock in a box stored beneath a bed. The bag is not a guarantee. It is a postponement of the moment when we decide that usefulness has ended and memory has nothing left to offer.

I have come to think of a pair as a temporary agreement rather than a permanent fact. Two socks belong together because we place them together, wash them together, and put them in the same drawer. The relationship is renewed each time we do the laundry. It is not written into the socks themselves. It is produced by habit, by convenience, and by the belief that objects can remain associated even when they are separated.

That belief is occasionally wrong. A sock can be lost. A key can become useless. A person can move away, taking one part of an arrangement and leaving another part behind in a drawer. The ordinary world is full of partial connections. We are not always able to recover what belonged with what, and we are not always supposed to.

The missing sock will probably not return. If it does, it will probably return at an inconvenient moment, perhaps weeks later, from a coat pocket or from the bottom of a bag. I will be pleased, though I will pretend that the surprise is less meaningful than it is. The case will be closed not because the mystery has been solved but because another mystery has arrived to take its place.

The dryer had made its argument. It knew nothing of pairs, only heat, motion, and time.

Its companion might have been in the courtyard, caught in a drain, carried away by someone who had no idea that a small domestic investigation was underway. The case will be closed not because the mystery has been solved but because another mystery has arrived to take its place.

For now, the blue sock is in the drawer. It is not broken, orphaned, or incomplete. It is simply a sock without its partner for the time being. The laundry will continue. The drawer will accumulate its small mismatches. And somewhere, in an apartment, a courtyard, a coat, or the folds of an ordinary day, the other sock may be waiting to be found.
